job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Aisha Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a bench by half past eight, testing heart-monitor circuit boards for a medical device company in Stockport. I follow a test plan, log the results and write up any board that fails, which is a lot of repeating the same report. I did electronic engineering at Manchester and scraped a pass, no placement, so I'm still proving myself to my lead, Kareem. I rent a room with two flatmates in Levenshulme and cook for all of us on Sundays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did the first few months go compared to what you imagined?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Better than I feared. My dad drives a taxi and my mum teaches, and they told me they'd cover any gap if I needed it, though I haven't. Hands-on testing is the best part, because a board either works or smokes. The write-ups are the dull part, and I've started asking an AI tool to tidy my wording now and then. I check everything it gives me, since in this trade a wrong sentence can mean a recall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but not magic. At work I'd tell Kareem it saves me ten minutes on a report and that's about it. To my friends I'd say the same, and that people should stop panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel steady. Hardware testing isn't going anywhere, because someone has to hold the probe. I'd still want the extra skills, since a pass degree and no placement doesn't make me stand out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep using the tool for write-ups and ask Kareem to let me help write test plans, not just run them. I'd put away 400 pounds a month and maybe look at a part-time course in medical device regulation. I'd also keep Sunday cooking, because it keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing dramatic, a bit of relief. The one thing I'd feel is impatience that I want to move up and the pace is slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you check what the tool gives you. Would that change if the tools got a little better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If I rely on the tool and get lazy, I'd lose the instinct for why a board failed. I'd make a rule for myself to write the first draft by hand on any strange failure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your life outside work that would worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Imogen, who is on a fixed-term contract in marketing. She'd be the one worried if things got rough. I'd say to her, honestly, that I'd back her for a few weeks if she needed it, because family helped me.

think: Hardware testing isn't going anywhere, since someone has to hold the **probe**.
A pass degree with no placement doesn't make me **stand out**.
do: Keep using the tool for **write-ups** and ask to help write test plans.
Save **400 pounds** a month and look at a medical device rules course.
feel: **Calm**, with some impatience to move up faster.

fieldNote: Her work is half **hands-on**, so she feels less exposed than pure desk staff.
Uses AI as an assistant and checks it, which fits a steady adopter.
Wants to stand out despite a plain degree.

steps.text: Ask Kareem to let me help write test plans
Use the AI tool for write-up wording and check each line
Save 400 pounds a month in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and companies owe their people a plan. I'd say publicly that firms using AI to cut graduate hiring are shifting the cost onto young people. I'd back stronger rules on how it's used in medical devices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the report-writing and the plan-checking go first, and that's most of what a junior does when the bench is empty. The bench work stays longer. I could end up as one of few juniors kept, or one of many not hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a day a week on the bench and the test-plan side, because those are less exposed. I'd take the regulatory course, about 600 pounds, since rules for medical gear are human-led for a long time. I'd also write down what I'm good at and ask for a performance review sooner than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm fine for now and I know it, but I can see the ground shifting. I'd want to be ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks do you think goes to software first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my firm uses an AI to read test logs and flag failures, my job becomes watching it. I'd ask to be the person who validates it, because someone must sign off, and that's a skill. Kareem would likely say yes since he's short-staffed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be hurt most by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The graduates who come in next year. If the firm stops hiring juniors, the next graduates would have no way in. I'd tell the managers they're eating their own seed corn.

say: Firms using AI to cut graduate hiring are shifting the **cost** onto young people.
I'd back **stronger** rules for AI in medical devices.

I could be one of few juniors **kept**, or one of many never hired.
do: Ask for one day a week on the **bench** and test plans.
Take the **regulatory** course for about 600 pounds.
Ask Kareem to make me the person who **validates** any AI log reader.
feel: **Uneasy**: fine for now, but I can see the ground shifting.

steps.text: Ask for one bench day a week and test-plan work
Pay for the medical device regulation course

Write to my MP about AI rules for graduate hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules and public support right now: a jobs guarantee, and tax on companies that replace workers. I'd say it quietly at work and loudly online. Two years is not time for people to adjust by themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. If AI does the thinking by 2028, my reports and test plans are gone, and the robots reach the bench by 2031. I might get three years of bench work, which is not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my spending to the bone and save about 1,000 pounds a month. I'd ask Kareem what the firm plans, and I'd join a union, probably the engineering one, within the first month. I'd also tell my parents and look at nursing or technician courses that run on human contact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not hopeless, because I have savings and my parents, but I don't see where an electronics graduate goes. It's a lot to hold at 22.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in month one compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Month one I'd stop the holiday I'd planned and I'd join the union. In the slow pictures I'd do the course first. Here there's no time to study something that'll be useless in the same two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them: I'm fine, I've saved, and I'm not coming home, but I might need the room later. My mum would say it's okay, my dad would try to give me money anyway. If my dad offers money I'd take it, because pride is a poor plan.

say: Two years is not enough time for people to adjust by **themselves**.
I'd say we need a **jobs guarantee** and tax on firms that replace workers.
think: If AI does the thinking by 2028, my reports and test plans are **gone**.
The bench might give me three years, which isn't a **career**.
do: Cut spending and save about **1,000 pounds** a month.

feel: **Anxious** and frightened, though savings and family give me some control.
S2.quote: If my dad offers money I'd take it, because pride is a poor plan.
fieldNote: Fear is real but **savings** and parents keep her short of panic.
Moves to collective action fast, which fits her politics.
Considers a **sharp** change of field, not a slow reskill.

steps.text: Cut spending and save 1,000 pounds a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do it properly: retraining funds, new rules and a share of the profits for ordinary people. I'd tell friends to save and to learn something that sits next to machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel I can cope. By 27 I could have a master's or a certificate in medical device safety, and that kind of job needs a human who signs. Still, I'm aware a lot of my peers won't be that lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the regulatory course next spring, then a part-time master's in biomedical engineering in year two. I'd keep working at the firm and ask for the validation role. I'd cut my savings goal slightly to pay fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though in a useful way. It pushes me to plan, and I like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the years while the bench is still human?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the bench stays human until 2034, I'd be one of the few able to do it and also understand the AI side. That's where I want to be. I'd ask Kareem to put me on the new test rig first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you worried about in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Imogen, my flatmate, would be the one I'd worry about, since she has no savings behind her. I'd probably help her find a short course and share my notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if governments use it, and I'd push for them to. I'd back a public retraining scheme and a way to share what AI makes. I'd tell my friends that now's the time to vote for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel okay. I can finish a master's, move into design or regulation and probably still be in work at 32. The thing I'd keep in mind is that the junior ladder might shrink before the big date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, take a part-time master's, and try to move to design or compliance within three years. I'd use AI tools more at work, since I'm steady and get used to them once others do. I'd also start saving for a flat, with a deposit from my own pay plus a bit from my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a thread of unease. Ten years is long enough that I can't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what does your life look like at 32?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 32 I'd like to be leading a small test team and maybe have a child. A decade lets me think about that, which two years wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you even though there's plenty of time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the plan depends on governments acting. If governments sit on their hands for eight years and then rush, I'd have a long calm stretch and then a very bad two years. I'd rather keep my skills ready than trust that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is too short for me to retrain and for the government to act. What would help is a public retraining fund, rules on cutting graduate hiring and the chance to be the person who checks the AI at work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age are told to be flexible, as if it's a personal fault. It's not our job to fix the system alone.

headlineQuote: People my age are told to be flexible, as if it's a personal fault.
portrait: Aisha is **22**, a junior test engineer for a medical device maker in Stockport, with a pass degree in electronic engineering.
She has savings and parents behind her and uses AI **now and then**, always checking its output.
She leans left and trusts rules, unions and **public** retraining over firms' good will.
Her mood runs calm, uneasy, anxious, uneasy, calm, and she turns exposure into a plan such as the **validation** role.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years is too short to **retrain** or for government to act.
whatWouldHelp: A public **retraining** fund, rules on graduate hiring cuts and a role checking the AI at work.
